title: Session 6: Practice
text:
The brief
186 cafés, 12 quarters. Each adopts a resident cat in quarter 4, 7 or 10. The outcome is average customer dwell time in minutes.

Deliverable: an estimate of the effect of adopting a cat, with a design statement, an event study, and an explicit list of what your data cannot answer.


Every planted effect in this dataset is positive and growing. The estimator most people reach for first returns a significant negative number. You will get the wrong answer on purpose, and then work out why.

section: Stage 1 · Get the wrong answer — 15 min
text:
Stage 1 · Get the wrong answer — 15 min
import essentials as ess
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

d = ess.load("cat_cafe")
twfe = smf.ols("dwell_min ~ has_cat + C(cafe_id) + C(quarter)", data=d).fit()


Plot mean dwell_min by quarter, one line per cohort. Does anything look wrong?
Report the has_cat coefficient, its standard error, its \(t\) and its \(p\).
Compare with ess.cat_cafe_truth(). What was planted?
Write one sentence describing what a careless analyst would now publish.



Do step 1 before step 2. The raw data looks entirely reasonable, and that is part of the lesson — nothing in the plot warns you.

title: Session 6: Practice
text:
Stage 2 · Find out why — 25 min
import diff_diff as dd

bacon = dd.BaconDecomposition().fit(
    d, outcome="dwell_min", unit="cafe_id", time="quarter",
    first_treat="cat_arrival_quarter")
bacon.to_dataframe()


Print the decomposition. How many 2×2 comparisons is TWFE averaging?
Confirm the weighted sum reproduces the TWFE estimate. To how many decimals?
Group the comparisons by type. What weight sits on each, and what is each type’s average estimate?
Look at the later_vs_earlier rows. Which cafés are serving as the control group in those comparisons?
Explain in three or four sentences why that produces a negative number when the true effects are positive and growing.



Step 5 is the single most important thing in this session. Write it out properly, in your own words — if you cannot, you do not have it yet.

For the post-treatment cells: how many land within two standard errors of the planted value?

What does control_group="not_yet_treated" change, mechanically?

title: Session 6: Practice
text:
Stage 4 · The event study — 15 min


Add an event_time column: quarter minus adoption quarter.
Average the estimates by event_time and plot them with confidence intervals, with the planted truth overlaid.
Are the pre-treatment estimates flat? Report their mean and the largest absolute value.
How many of the placebo cells are individually significant at 5%? Now: how many would you expect, given how many tests you just ran?



Step 4 is a lesson about pre-trend tests generally. They are a multiple-testing problem, and reading them one star at a time will make you reject good designs.

section: Stage 5 · What you cannot know — 10 min
text:
Stage 5 · What you cannot know — 10 min


Some post-treatment cells come back as NA. Which, and how many?
Why? Count how many cafés are untreated in quarter 11.
TWFE reported a number for those same quarters. Where did it get it?
Compute a breakdown value: how large a differential trend, in minutes per quarter, would be needed to drive your estimate to zero? Compare it with the pre-treatment trend you can actually measure.
Write the design recommendation: what should the cafés have done differently so this study could evaluate its own last phase?

title: Session 6: Before the session
text:
2 · Potential outcomes
For each unit \(i\), imagine two numbers:



\(Y_i(1)\)
the outcome if treated


\(Y_i(0)\)
the outcome if not treated



The causal effect for that unit is \(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\).

You never observe both. A café either has a cat or it does not, so exactly half of every unit’s causal information is missing by construction. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference, and no dataset solves it.

title: Session 6: Before the session
text:
What we estimate instead
We give up on individual effects and estimate an average:
\[ \text{ATT} = \mathbb{E}\left[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid \text{treated}\right] \]
the average effect on the treated. To get it, we need a stand-in for \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid \text{treated}]\) — the outcome the treated units would have had. That stand-in is what every method in this session is arguing about.

A causal claim is always a claim about a counterfactual, and a counterfactual is never in your data. The design is the argument for the substitute you used.

3 · The 2×2 difference-in-differences
Two groups, two periods. One group gets treated in between.




before
after
change




treated
50

+35


control
35
55
+20





DiD = +15





The treated group rose by 35. That is not the effect: things were changing anyway.
The control group rose by 20. That is our estimate of what would have happened to the treated group without treatment.
The difference of the differences is 15.

title: Session 6: Before the session
section: The same number, as a regression
text:
The same number, as a regression
\[ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Treated} + \beta_2\,\text{Post} + \beta_3\,(\text{Treated}\times\text{Post}) + \varepsilon \]



\(\beta_0\)
control group, before


\(\beta_1\)
how much higher the treated group started


\(\beta_2\)
how much everyone changed over time


\(\beta_3\)
the DiD estimate




The interaction is the estimate. Work through the table above and confirm that \(\beta_0 = 35\), \(\beta_1 = 15\), \(\beta_2 = 20\), \(\beta_3 = 15\). Do it on paper — it is fifteen minutes that makes the rest of the session readable.

title: Session 6: Before the session
text:
4 · Parallel trends
The assumption doing all the work:

In the absence of treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trend.



It does not require the two groups to be similar. Levels can differ freely — \(\beta_1\) absorbs that.
It does require their changes to have matched.
It is fundamentally untestable, because it is a statement about a counterfactual.



What you can do is check whether trends matched before treatment, and treat that as evidence about the period after. That is the event study, and it is evidence rather than proof.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
What session 5 is for


The mathematics

The Bayes classifier: \(\arg\max_j \Pr(Y=j \mid x)\), and its irreducible rate
\(k\)-NN estimates that posterior by local averaging
\(k\) controls the bias–variance trade directly
Distance in an irrelevant dimension is still distance


The Python

KNeighborsClassifier, and why StandardScaler is compulsory
GridSearchCV over \(k\), on training data only
confusion_matrix and classification_report
Drawing a decision boundary on a mesh


The judgement

Use a known ceiling to detect leakage rather than to celebrate
Refuse accuracy as a headline on imbalanced classes
Choose between precision and recall from the problem, not the metric
Say what a method cannot do, not just how it scored

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
The data

d = ess.load("bestiary")
print(d.species.value_counts().to_string())
print(f"\nrarest species: {(d.species == 'ember_drake').mean():.2%} of records")

species
thornback      545
glimmerwing    527
dusk_moth      494
ember_drake     34

rarest species: 2.12% of records



Two measurements carry real information — wing span and tail length. mass_g, antenna_mm and scale_count are noise, and we come back to them at the end.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
What the classes look like


The clouds overlap. That overlap is not a measurement problem — it is the reason perfect classification is impossible here, and it puts a hard ceiling on every method in this session.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
The Bayes classifier
If you knew the true class probabilities at every point, the best rule would be to predict the most likely class:
\[ \hat y(x) = \arg\max_j \Pr(Y = j \mid X = x) \]
This data is generated from four known Gaussians with known priors, so that posterior is computable:

post = ess.bestiary_posterior(d.wing_span_cm, d.tail_length_cm)
bayes_pred = np.array(SPECIES)[post.argmax(1)]

print(f"Bayes accuracy          {accuracy_score(y, bayes_pred):.4f}")
print(f"Bayes balanced accuracy {balanced_accuracy_score(y, bayes_pred):.4f}")

Bayes accuracy          0.8625
Bayes balanced accuracy 0.8876

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
What that number is for

0.8625 is the ceiling. No classifier — not a neural network, not a billion rows — can do better on this data, because the classes genuinely overlap and 7% of the field identifications are wrong.


So a test accuracy of 0.99 would not be an achievement. It would be a bug report: test rows leaking into training, or a feature that encodes the answer.
Most real problems do not hand you the floor. Estimating one anyway — from a simple baseline, from measurement reliability, from what a human expert achieves — turns an unanchored score into a number you can interpret.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
The whole algorithm
To classify a new point: find the \(k\) closest training points, take a vote.
\[ \hat{\Pr}(Y = j \mid x) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in N_k(x)} \mathbb{1}(y_i = j) \]


No fitting. No coefficients, no likelihood, no optimisation.
No functional form. It never assumes linearity, or normality, or anything.
Everything is stored. Prediction costs a search over the training set.

title: Session 5: Classification
section: Standardise, or the units decide for you
text:
Standardise, or the units decide for you

print("raw scales:")
print(d[["wing_span_cm", "tail_length_cm", "mass_g", "scale_count"]]
      .std().round(2).to_string())

raw scales:
wing_span_cm       2.20
tail_length_cm     2.53
mass_g            45.01
scale_count       64.13



mass_g has a standard deviation nearly twenty times that of tail length. In Euclidean distance it would swamp everything else — and it is pure noise. A distance-based method with unstandardised features is measuring whatever happens to have the biggest numbers.

\(k = 1\) against \(k = 400\)

for k in (1, 5, 15, 45, 125, 400):
    m = KNeighborsClassifier(k).fit(A, ytr)

print(f"\nBayes floor: {BAYES:.3f}")

k =    1   train 0.999   test 0.762
k =    5   train 0.866   test 0.850
k =   15   train 0.858   test 0.867
k =   45   train 0.855   test 0.873
k =  125   train 0.838   test 0.854
k =  400   train 0.829   test 0.850

Bayes floor: 0.863



Read the two columns as a pair. At \(k = 1\) the model knows the training data perfectly and generalises worst. At \(k = 400\) it has stopped distinguishing anything. The best test score sits in the middle, just about at the floor.

title: Session 5: Classification
section: Three boundaries, and the truth underneath
text:
Three boundaries, and the truth underneath


Colour is what the classifier learnt; the black lines are the true boundary.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
Read those three panels


\(k = 1\) — the colour regions are shattered into islands, many of them a single mislabelled creature. The classifier has learnt the 7% label noise. Perfect on training data, worst on new data. Variance.
\(k = 45\) — the coloured regions follow the black lines closely. This is what “close to the truth” looks like.
\(k = 400\) — smooth, and in the wrong place. The rare species has vanished entirely from the map. Bias.



The bias–variance trade is not an abstraction here. It is three pictures, and you can see which one is right because the answer is drawn underneath.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
Choosing \(k\) honestly
You cannot choose \(k\) on the test set — that would make the test score an estimate of nothing. Cross-validate within the training data:

grid = GridSearchCV(KNeighborsClassifier(),
                    {"n_neighbors": list(range(1, 151, 2))},
                    cv=KFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).fit(A, ytr)

print(f"best k by CV      {grid.best_params_['n_neighbors']}")
print(f"CV accuracy       {grid.best_score_:.4f}")
print(f"test accuracy     {grid.score(B, yte):.4f}")
print(f"Bayes floor       {BAYES:.4f}")

best k by CV      21
CV accuracy       0.8580
test accuracy     0.8688
Bayes floor       0.8625



CV picked 21, not the 45 that happened to win on the test set. Both land within a percentage point of the floor, and the difference between them is noise. Picking the \(k\) that maximised the test score would have been cheating for nothing.

QDA (curved — the correct family)        train 0.853  test 0.875
decision tree, depth 3                   train 0.825  test 0.844
decision tree, unlimited                 train 0.999  test 0.765
k-NN, k = 45                             train 0.855  test 0.873

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
What that table says


QDA is the right family — the data really is a mixture of Gaussians with unequal covariances — and it lands at 0.875, at the floor. It wins by knowing the answer’s shape.
\(k\)-NN gets there too, at 0.873, without knowing anything. That is the case for a non-parametric method.
The linear boundary loses almost nothing (0.867). Worth noticing: curvature only costs you where the data actually is, and here it barely is.
The unlimited tree is \(k=1\) again: train 0.999, test 0.765.



Two models can score identically for opposite reasons. Reporting only the score hides which.

The number that ends the argument

print(f"the model as fitted              {accuracy_score(yte, pred):.4f}")
print(f"the same model, ember drakes      "

      f"{accuracy_score(yte, pred) - accuracy_score(yte, blind):.4f}")

Total blindness to the rare species costs 1.7 percentage points of accuracy. If accuracy is your objective, the optimiser has almost no reason to find it — and if the rare species is the one you built the classifier for, accuracy is measuring the wrong thing.

title: Session 5: Classification
section: Which of those two do you need?
text:
Which of those two do you need?








Precision
\(TP/(TP+FP)\)
of the ones I flagged, how many deserved it?


Recall
\(TP/(TP+FN)\)
of the ones that existed, how many did I find?




For ember_drake: precision 1.000, recall 0.800. Every drake it named was a drake; it found four in five. Whether that is a good classifier depends entirely on what happens next.



Cataloguing a rare species for conservation → recall. A missed drake is a drake that goes unprotected; a false alarm costs a field visit.
Triggering an expensive intervention → precision. A false alarm wastes the budget.



macro avg gives each class equal weight regardless of size; weighted avg reproduces accuracy. On imbalanced data the macro average — or balanced accuracy — is usually the honest headline.

title: Session 5: Classification
section: Why noise hurts a distance method
text:
Why noise hurts a distance method

\(k\)-NN asks “who is nearby?” In five dimensions, two creatures of the same species can be pushed apart by nothing more than a difference in mass — and distance in an irrelevant dimension is still distance. The neighbourhood fills up with the wrong neighbours.



This is the curse of dimensionality in miniature. As dimensions grow, all points become roughly equidistant and “nearby” stops meaning anything.
A regression would have shrunk those coefficients towards zero. \(k\)-NN has no coefficients, so it cannot ignore a feature you give it.
Which is why feature selection matters more for distance methods than for penalised linear ones.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
Importance without coefficients
\(k\)-NN has nothing to report as an effect size. To find out what a feature is worth, scramble it and see what breaks:

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

m5 = KNeighborsClassifier(45).fit(nsc.transform(Ntr), nytr)
imp = permutation_importance(m5, nsc.transform(Nte), nyte,
                             n_repeats=12, random_state=0)
cols = ["wing_span_cm", "tail_length_cm", "mass_g", "antenna_mm", "scale_count"]
print(pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=cols)
        .sort_values(ascending=False).round(4).to_string())

tail_length_cm    0.3130
wing_span_cm      0.2627
mass_g            0.0057
antenna_mm        0.0035
scale_count       0.0007



The two real features carry all the importance; the three noise columns sit at roughly zero. Permutation importance is model-agnostic — it works for anything with a .predict, which is exactly what you need when there are no coefficients.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
What to report


The confusion matrix, always. Accuracy alone is not a result.
Accuracy against a baseline — the majority class, and a floor if you can estimate one.
Per-class precision and recall, and which one your problem needs.
How the hyperparameter was chosen, and on which data.
What the model cannot do.



A single accuracy figure, with no baseline, no confusion matrix and no statement of how the hyperparameter was chosen, is not a finding. It is a number.

title: Session 5: Classification
text:
Key takeaways


Know the ceiling if you can compute one. It turns a high score from good news into a question.
\(k\)-NN has no fit, no form and no coefficients. The training data is the model.
\(k\) is the bias–variance dial: \(k=1\) is memorisation, \(k=n\) is the majority class.
Standardise. A distance method with mixed units is measuring the units.
Accuracy hides rare classes. Ignoring a 2% class costs 1.7 points; the confusion matrix shows it and accuracy does not.

title: Session 4: Before the session
text:
2 · The shape of the problem
Every model so far had many more rows than columns. This session starts with the opposite: 60 rows, 200 columns.

When \(p > n\), the matrix \(X^\top X\) is singular. There is no unique least-squares solution — there are infinitely many, and every one of them fits the training data perfectly, with zero residuals.


This is not a numerical inconvenience. A model that fits perfectly has learnt the noise, and it will predict new data badly. The way out is to stop asking for the best fit, and deliberately accept a worse one.

title: Session 4: Before the session
text:
3 · Bias and variance
Take the expected squared prediction error at a point and decompose it:
\[ \mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat f(x))^2\right] = \underbrace{\text{Bias}^2}_{\text{wrong on average}} + \underbrace{\text{Variance}}_{\text{unstable}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}} \]







Bias
how far the average fit is from the truth. High for models too simple to represent it.


Variance
how much the fit moves if you resample the data. High for flexible models.


\(\sigma^2\)
noise. No method removes it, and no method should appear to.

title: Session 4: Before the session
section: The trade you are about to make
text:
The trade you are about to make

Least squares is unbiased. That sounds like a virtue, and with \(p\) close to \(n\) it is a disaster: unbiasedness is bought with enormous variance, and total error is what you care about.


Every method in this session adds bias on purpose to buy a larger reduction in variance. A deliberately wrong estimator that predicts better is not a paradox; it is the whole design.

title: Session 4: Before the session
text:
4 · Cross-validation
You cannot choose how much to shrink using the data you fitted on: more flexibility always fits better. So hold data back.
\(k\)-fold cross-validation. Split the rows into \(k\) parts. For each part: fit on the other \(k-1\), predict the held-out part, record the error. Average.
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score

kf = KFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=kf, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")

shuffle=True matters. Without it, KFold takes contiguous blocks, and if your rows are sorted by anything at all the folds are not exchangeable.

title: Session 4: Before the session

What cross-validation is optimising

It estimates prediction error. That is worth saying twice, because this session’s puzzle turns on it: the penalty that predicts best is not the penalty that identifies the right variables. Cross-validation will hand you a model with too many variables in it, and it will be right to.

title: Session 3: Logistic Regression
text:
What we fit, and why
A linear model on a 0/1 outcome produces predicted probabilities above 1 and below 0. So model the log-odds, which are free to be any real number:
\[ \log\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k \]
and invert to recover a probability:
\[ p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}, \qquad \eta = \beta_0 + \textstyle\sum_j \beta_j x_j \]

There is no closed-form solution. The coefficients are found by maximum likelihood — numerically, by iteration — which is why the output reports a log-likelihood rather than an \(R^2\).

Several at once: the likelihood-ratio test
To test whether a group of variables belongs — all three habitat levels, say — compare log-likelihoods:
\[ 2\left(\ell_{\text{full}} - \ell_{\text{restricted}}\right) \sim \chi^2_{\Delta k} \]

from scipy import stats

reduced = smf.logit(
    F.replace(" + C(habitat, Treatment('grassland'))", ""), data=d).fit(disp=0)

lr = 2 * (fit.llf - reduced.llf)
df = int(fit.df_model - reduced.df_model)
print(f"LR statistic {lr:.2f} on {df} df,  p = {stats.chi2.sf(lr, df):.2e}")

title: Session 3: Logistic Regression
section: The two errors are not the same size
text:
The two errors are not the same size







False negative
you call it edible, it is poisonous. A hospital visit.


False positive
you call it poisonous, it was edible. A discarded mushroom.




Say a hospital visit is 50 times worse than losing a mushroom. Then expected loss is \(c_{FN} \times FN + c_{FP} \times FP\), and it is minimised at
\[ t^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}} = \frac{1}{51} = 0.0196 \]


Accuracy is the special case where the two costs are equal. It is a strange assumption, and it is almost never stated out loud.

section: Does the theory hold on our data?

title: Session 3: Logistic Regression
text:
The loss curve



theory       t = 0.0196   loss 630
empirical    t = 0.0305   loss 614
within 5% of the minimum:  t in [0.0210, 0.0305]



The two do not coincide exactly, and they should not: with 1,400 discrete cases the loss is a step function, so its minimum is a flat region rather than a point. Theory names 0.0196; the empirical floor runs from about 0.021 to 0.031, and the loss at the theoretical value is within 3% of the best achievable.


The formula is a guide to the right neighbourhood, not a value to quote to four decimal places. What matters is that it puts you two orders of magnitude away from 0.5.

The cost-optimal rule has worse accuracy — 0.585 against 0.877 — and cuts expected loss by a factor of eight. It discards 70% of the basket and misses one poisonous mushroom in four hundred.

The ROC curve is the whole menu


AUC summarises the curve over every threshold, which is why it is a good measure of the model and a bad basis for a decision. You do not deploy a curve; you deploy a point on it.

text:
Edible, upset stomach, hospital, fatal
Those four are ordered, and collapsing them to a binary throws that away. An ordinal (proportional-odds) model uses one set of coefficients and a set of cut-points:
\[ \log\frac{\Pr(Y \le j)}{\Pr(Y > j)} = \alpha_j - \textstyle\sum_k \beta_k x_k \]

from statsmodels.miscmodels.ordinal_model import OrderedModel

sub = d.dropna(subset=["toxicity"]).copy()
X = pd.get_dummies(
    sub[["odor_index", "volva_present", "ring_present", "spore_print"]],
    columns=["spore_print"], drop_first=True, dtype=float)

    method="bfgs", disp=0)

title: Session 3: Logistic Regression
text:
What that model assumes

One coefficient per variable, shared across all the thresholds. The effect of a volva on the odds of “at least upset stomach” is assumed identical to its effect on the odds of “fatal”. That is the proportional-odds assumption, and it is what buys you the parsimony.


If it is false — if a feature predicts mild illness but not death — the model will average the two and report something true of neither. Check it by fitting separate binary logits at each cut-point and comparing the coefficients. If they diverge, use a multinomial model and give up the ordering.

title: Session 3: Logistic Regression
text:
What to report


Coefficients as odds ratios, with intervals
The confusion matrix, not accuracy alone — and always against the majority-class baseline
The threshold you chose and the costs that justify it
Which error you deliberately made more of
AUC for the model; a chosen point on the ROC curve for the decision



A classifier reported without its threshold, or a threshold reported without its costs, is an unfinished piece of work.

title: Session 3: Logistic Regression
text:
Key takeaways


Model the log-odds; recover probabilities by inverting.
\(e^{\beta}\) is an odds ratio. It is constant; the probability change it implies is not.
Accuracy is a trap on imbalanced data. Always quote the majority-class baseline beside it.
The threshold is a decision that belongs to the costs, not to the model. \(t^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\).
The best decision rule can have the worse accuracy. If that sounds wrong, the metric is wrong.
Ordinal models buy parsimony with the proportional-odds assumption. Check it.

Why question 4 matters

If each baker works at a different hydration, then “hydration” and “which baker” are partly the same variable. Any effect you attribute to one could belong to the other, and the regression has no way to tell them apart unless you let it.


That is the trap in this session’s data, and it costs about four percentage points of hydration in the final answer. Come to class knowing the bakers are not interchangeable.

title: Session 2: Before the session
section: 3 · Three shapes a line cannot make
text:
3 · Three shapes a line cannot make
A hill
Rise increases with hydration, then decreases. There is a best value, and a straight line will tell you the best value is at whichever edge of the data it is sloping towards.

The fix: a squared term. \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2\), with \(\beta_2 < 0\) for a hill. The peak sits at \(-\beta_1 / 2\beta_2\).

title: Session 2: Before the session
section: Three shapes a line cannot make (cont.)
text:
Three shapes a line cannot make (cont.)
A slope that depends on something else
The best oven temperature might be different for wet dough than for dry dough. That is not two separate effects — it is one effect conditional on the other.

The fix: an interaction. hydration_pct:oven_c in a formula, or hydration_pct*oven_c for the two main effects and the interaction together.

A level that differs by group
One baker’s loaves rise 9 mm more than another’s, for reasons no column records: their oven, their hands, their kitchen.

The fix: fixed effects. C(baker) adds one dummy per baker and one intercept each, and the other coefficients are then estimated within bakers.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
What we are fitting
\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i \]
Least squares picks the \(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1\) that make the sum of squared vertical distances as small as possible:
\[ \hat\beta = \arg\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2 \]

Squared, so that being 4 too high is four times worse than being 2 too high, not twice. Vertical, so the method assumes \(x\) is known and \(y\) is the thing with error in it.

title: Session 1: Regression
section: What the scatter already told us
text:
What the scatter already told us
Two things, before a single model was fitted:


The main cloud bends. It rises steeply at first and flattens out. A straight line through it will not sit right.
Six points sit well above everything else: high speed from a small drop. They are the ones marked launch.



Fit the whole thing anyway and you get \(R^2\) = 0.46 — mediocre, and the number gives no hint as to which of the two problems caused it.


So we set the six aside provisionally, and come back at the end of the session to justify it with a diagnostic rather than with a glance. Setting rows aside because you looked at a picture is a hypothesis, not a finding.

title: Session 1: Regression
section: Reading that, one column at a time
text:
Reading that, one column at a time


coefficient     0.9397   km/h per metre of drop
std error       0.0210   how much it would wobble on new data
t                44.79   coefficient / std error
95% interval  [0.898, 0.982]




The coefficient has units. 0.940 km/h per metre of drop. A coaster with a drop 10 m larger is predicted 9.4 km/h faster.
The standard error is the honest part. It says how much of that number is the data and how much is luck.
The \(t\)-statistic is a ratio. It has no units, and on its own it tells you nothing about whether the effect matters.

And now \(R^2\)

Ninety-six per cent of the variance in top speed, from one variable. In most fields you would stop here and write it up.


This model is still wrong. Not imprecise — wrong in shape, and \(R^2\) has no way of telling you so. We removed the six rows that were obviously a different mechanism, and the remaining problem is the one \(R^2\) cannot see.

text:
The one plot to draw first
A residual is what the model failed to explain: \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\).
Plot the residuals against the fitted values. If the model has the shape right, there is no pattern — the residuals are a formless band around zero. Any structure you can see is signal the model left on the table.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2))
ax.scatter(lin.fittedvalues, lin.resid, s=16, alpha=0.75, color=CL.ink)
ax.axhline(0, color=CL.muted, lw=1)

ax.set_ylabel("Residual (km/h)")

What that plot is telling you
The band is not formless. It rises, peaks, and comes back down — an arch. Bin the residuals and the arch is unmistakable:

bands = pd.cut(g.drop_m, [0, 25, 45, 65, 85, 105, 200])

       .agg(["mean", "count"]).round(2))

Small drops: the model over-predicts. Middling drops: it under-predicts. Large drops: it over-predicts again. A straight line is being asked to trace a curve, and it is splitting the difference.

title: Session 1: Regression
section: Confirm it with a test, not just an eye
text:
Confirm it with a test, not just an eye

quad = smf.ols("speed_kmh ~ drop_m + I(drop_m**2)", data=g).fit()
t = quad.tvalues["I(drop_m ** 2)"]
print(f"quadratic term:  t = {t:.2f},  p = {quad.pvalues['I(drop_m ** 2)']:.2e}")
print(f"linear R2 {lin.rsquared:.4f}  ->  quadratic R2 {quad.rsquared:.4f}")

quadratic term:  t = -8.57,  p = 9.82e-13
linear R2 0.9635  ->  quadratic R2 0.9816



\(p \approx 10^{-12}\). The curvature is not a matter of taste. I(...) means “treat what is inside as arithmetic, not as formula syntax” — without it, ** would be read as an interaction.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
Where the curve comes from
A car that falls a height \(h\) converts potential energy into kinetic energy:
\[ mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{2gh} \]
Speed goes as the square root of the drop. That is why a straight line could not fit it, and no amount of extra data would have helped.

The fix is not a better line. It is a different functional form.

title: Session 1: Regression
section: Logs turn a power law into a straight line
text:
Logs turn a power law into a straight line
If \(v = c\,h^{k}\) then taking logs of both sides gives
\[ \log v = \log c + k \log h \]
which is a straight line whose slope is the exponent. So regress \(\log v\) on \(\log h\) and read \(k\) off directly.

g["log_speed"] = np.log(g.speed_kmh)
g["log_drop"]  = np.log(g.drop_m)

power = smf.ols("log_speed ~ log_drop", data=g).fit()
k, klo, khi = power.params["log_drop"], *power.conf_int().loc["log_drop"]
print(f"exponent  k = {k:.4f}   95% CI [{klo:.4f}, {khi:.4f}]")
print(f"R2 = {power.rsquared:.4f}")

exponent  k = 0.4971   95% CI [0.4835, 0.5106]
R2 = 0.9859

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
Read that interval


theory says      k = 0.5      (v proportional to sqrt(h))
the data says    k = 0.4971   95% CI [0.4835, 0.5106]
and the constant   c = 15.17
frictionless      3.6*sqrt(2g) = 15.95



The confidence interval contains 0.5 and excludes 1. The regression has recovered a law of physics from a spreadsheet of theme-park statistics.


The constant comes in below the frictionless value because real track loses energy. Friction costs speed; it does not change the exponent.

text:
The two models, side by side


Both fit well. Only one of them means something.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
Three different things



Outlier
unusual \(y\), given its \(x\). Badly predicted.


Leverage point
unusual \(x\). Has the power to move the line.


Influential
actually moves it. Needs both.




A point far from the centre of \(x\) but sitting exactly on the line does no damage. A badly predicted point in the middle of the data does very little either. The damage is done by points that are both.

title: Session 1: Regression
section: Leverage, and the fact that it sums to \(p\)
text:
Leverage, and the fact that it sums to \(p\)
Leverage is the diagonal of the hat matrix \(H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\), and \(h_{ii}\) is how much \(\hat y_i\) responds to \(y_i\). Its total is fixed:
\[ \sum_i h_{ii} = \operatorname{trace}(H) = p \]

full = smf.ols("log_speed ~ log_drop",
               data=d.assign(log_speed=np.log(d.speed_kmh),
                             log_drop=np.log(d.drop_m))).fit()
inf = full.get_influence()
h = inf.hat_matrix_diag

print(f"sum of leverages   {h.sum():.6f}   (p = {int(full.df_model + 1)})")
print(f"mean leverage      {h.mean():.4f}   = p/n")
print(f"2p/n screen        {2 * 2 / len(d):.4f}   {(h > 2*2/len(d)).sum()} above it")

sum of leverages   2.000000   (p = 2)
mean leverage      0.0238   = p/n
2p/n screen        0.0476   6 above it



There is a fixed budget of influence, and every observation gets a share. Adding rows does not create more; it divides the same total more finely.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
Cook’s distance
Cook’s distance asks the question you actually care about: if I deleted this row, how far would all the fitted values move?
\[ D_i = \frac{\sum_j (\hat y_j - \hat y_{j(i)})^2}{p\,\hat\sigma^2} \]
It combines leverage with the size of the residual, which is why it is the one number to look at rather than either on its own.

cooks = inf.cooks_distance[0]
print(f"largest Cook's D   {cooks.max():.4f}")
print(f"above 4/n ({4/len(d):.4f}):  {(cooks > 4/len(d)).sum()} of {len(d)} rows")

largest Cook's D   0.6875
above 4/n (0.0476):  6 of 84 rows

top = np.argsort(cooks)[-6:][::-1]

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
What the diagnostic found
Five of the six most influential observations are launched coasters — propelled by hydraulics or linear motors instead of being dropped.

Energy conservation says nothing about them. They reach 240 km/h from a 40-metre structure because a motor put the energy in. They are not outliers in the sense of bad measurements. They are a different physical system, and they should never have been in the regression.


This is the sequence to internalise: a diagnostic points at rows → you go and read the rows → the rows tell you the model was mis-specified. The diagnostic did not tell you to delete anything. It told you where to look.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
What keeping them costs

print(f"gravity only (n={len(g)}):  k = {k:.4f}")
print(f"all 84 coasters:        k = {full.params['log_drop']:.4f}")

gravity only (n=78):  k = 0.4971
all 84 coasters:        k = 0.3722



Six rows out of 84 — seven per cent of the data — move the exponent from 0.50 to 0.37, and 0.37 corresponds to no law of anything. The interval around it is narrow and confidently wrong.


And this is the justification we owed from the opening slide. We set those rows aside because a picture suggested it; we keep them aside because Cook’s distance identified them, the propulsion column explains them, and the physics says they belong to a different model.


Deleting rows is a modelling decision that has to be argued for. “They are a different mechanism, and here is the column that says so” is an argument. “They were far from the line” is not.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
What to report


The coefficient, in units, with its standard error or interval
The functional form, and why that one — not just that it fit better
What you looked for in the residuals, and what you found
Which observations you investigated, what they turned out to be, and what you did about them
What the result does not license you to claim



\(R^2\) is the least informative number in the output, and it is the one most often reported alone.

title: Session 1: Regression
text:
Key takeaways


A coefficient is a quantity with units. Say them.
\(R^2\) measures closeness, not correctness. A model can be very close and the wrong shape.
Residuals versus fitted, always. Curvature there means the form is wrong, and no amount of data fixes it.
Logs turn a power law into a line whose slope is the exponent.
Leverage is capacity; Cook’s distance is damage. Investigate the rows the diagnostics point at — then decide, and say what you decided.

title: Session 1: Before the session
section: Why VS Codium rather than VS Code
text:
Why VS Codium rather than VS Code
Visual Studio Code is developed in the open under a permissive licence. The binary Microsoft distributes is not the same artefact: it adds telemetry and ships under a proprietary licence, and its extension marketplace is a Microsoft service with its own terms. VS Codium is the identical source, compiled without the telemetry and the branding.

The practical reason is the habit rather than this course’s data. The teaching data here is generated on your laptop and could not matter less. The habit is for the working file you will one day open under a non-disclosure agreement or a research ethics protocol. An editor that reports usage to a third party should be a decision you make once, deliberately — not a default you inherited.

title: Session 1: Before the session
section: Why a local model rather than a hosted one
text:
Why a local model rather than a hosted one
The model you will install is Chinese, developed by Alibaba. It is worth being direct about that, because the reflex is to treat provenance as the security question, and here it is not.








Open weights, on your machine
It cannot send your data anywhere. There is no connection to send it over — and you can verify that rather than trust it: turn the wifi off and watch it keep working.


A closed model behind an API
Receives everything you type, by construction, wherever the company is domiciled.





On the dimension people actually care about — does my work leave this room — open weights running locally are the stronger guarantee, and the nationality of the developer does not enter into it.

title: Session 1: Before the session
text:
And why a small one
Qwen 2.5 Coder is a vertical model: specialised for code, and consequently far better at code, for its size, than a general assistant many times larger.


A 3-billion-parameter model on a laptop is not competitive with a frontier system at open-ended reasoning.
At completing a pandas idiom, or explaining what a function does, it is entirely adequate.



Choosing a small specialised model over a large general one — and knowing which tasks admit that trade — is the applied judgement that separates a sensible AI deployment from an expensive one. It is also, almost exactly, the judgement session 4 makes about a deliberately biased estimator.

What the model is for, and what it is not
You will read far more code this term than you write: the session decks, the starter scripts, your own work from three weeks ago. A model beside the file answers “what does this do” without your leaving the file.








Good use
Poor use




“Explain what this block does”
“Write my analysis”


“Why does this throw a KeyError?”
“Is this result significant?”


“What is the pandas idiom for this?”
“Interpret this coefficient for me”





The standing rule of this course. Every deliverable must document at least one instance where you identified a model output as wrong, unverifiable or misleading, and explain how you established that. You are never penalised for using the model. You are penalised for using it uncritically.


The honest limitation, stated once: on a machine without a graphics card, a small model is a capable reader and an unreliable editor. It will explain a function correctly and then fail to produce a well-formed multi-file edit, because emitting a precise diff is a harder task than describing code. That is a fact about small models rather than about you.

title: Session 1: Before the session
section: 10 · Enough inference to read a coefficient
text:
10 · Enough inference to read a coefficient
A regression hands you three numbers per variable. You need to know what each one is before you can be told a fourth.







Coefficient
how much \(y\) moves per one-unit move in \(x\) — in the units of \(y\)


Standard error
how much that estimate would wobble if you collected the data again


\(t\)-statistic
the coefficient divided by its standard error: how many wobbles from zero




A coefficient is a quantity with units. A \(t\)-statistic is a ratio, and has none. Reporting the second without the first is the most common way to say nothing at all.

title: Session 1: Before the session
text:
The \(p\)-value, stated carefully

If the true effect were exactly zero, and I repeated this whole study many times, what fraction of those studies would produce a coefficient at least this far from zero?

That is the \(p\)-value. It is a statement about data under an assumption, not about the probability that the assumption is true.

It does not tell you the effect is large. It does not tell you the effect is real. With 2,000 rows, an effect too small to care about will clear \(p < 0.05\) comfortably — and you would still be right not to care.

title: Session 1: Before the session
section: What \(R^2\) is, and what it is not
text:
What \(R^2\) is, and what it is not
\(R^2\) is the share of the variance in \(y\) that your fitted values reproduce. It runs from 0 to 1, and it rises whenever you add a variable — including a variable made of pure noise.

\(R^2\) measures how close the line is to the points. It says nothing about whether the line is the right shape.


Session 1’s puzzle is built precisely on that gap: a model with \(R^2 = 0.96\) that gets the answer wrong, sitting next to a model that gets it right. If you learn one thing before class, learn to distrust that number on its own.

The brief
You have 84 roller coasters. For each one: the height of its first drop, its top speed, its length, how many inversions it has, and how long the queue was when somebody measured it.

Two of those columns are connected by a physical law of the form \(v = c\,h^{k}\). Your job is to report \(k\), with an interval, and to say what \(c\) turned out to be.


There is a specific right answer. It is a number you can look up in a physics textbook, and you will know when you have it. Do not look it up first — the point is to recover it from data.

Stage 1 · Look, and fit — 15 min
import essentials as ess

d = ess.load("coasters")


Plot top speed against drop height. Actually plot it, before fitting.
Fit speed_kmh ~ drop_m and write down the coefficient in its units.
Write down \(R^2\).



Keep that \(R^2\) written down somewhere. You are going to need it later, when it turns out to have been no help at all.

title: Session 1: Practice
text:
Stage 2 · Diagnose it — 20 min


Plot residuals against fitted values.
Say in a sentence what structure you can see. Not “looks fine” — name the shape, and name what you were looking for.
Bin the residuals by drop height and take the mean in each bin. Does the sign of the mean residual change as you move across the range?
Add a squared term and test it. What does the \(p\)-value say?



If your answer to 2 is that there is no structure, look again. There is, and it is not subtle once you know to look for a change of sign.

title: Session 1: Practice
text:
Stage 3 · Find the law — 25 min
You are looking for \(v = c\,h^{k}\). Taking logs of both sides gives you something you already know how to fit.

\[\log v = \log c + k \log h\]
The slope of that regression is the exponent. The exponential of the intercept is \(c\).



Fit it. Report \(k\) with a 95% confidence interval.
Report \(c\).
Does your interval contain a simple fraction? Which one?
Now say what physical statement that fraction corresponds to.

inf = fit.get_influence()

cooks    = inf.cooks_distance[0]


Confirm that the leverages sum to \(p\). They do, exactly. Say why.
Find the six observations with the largest Cook’s distance.
Go and read those rows. Print them. What do they have in common?
Re-estimate \(k\) with and without them. Report both numbers.
Decide whether to keep them, and write down the argument — not the decision.



This stage carries the most marks. A group that can explain why those rows behave differently has understood the session; a group that deleted them because they were far from the line has not.

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
What session 2 is for


The mathematics

A quadratic has its optimum at \(-\beta_1/2\beta_2\)
With an interaction, \(\partial y/\partial x\) depends on \(z\)
Fixed effects estimate within groups, not across them
AIC trades fit against parameter count: \(-2\log L + 2k\)


The Python

I(x**2) for arithmetic inside a formula
x*z for main effects plus interaction; x:z for the interaction alone
C(group) for a full set of dummies
Locate an optimum from the coefficients, and check it numerically


The judgement

Say what a main effect means once an interaction is present
Notice when a group variable is confounded with your variable of interest
Report an optimum as a region, not a point
Refuse to read AIC as though the data had chosen the model

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
section: The obvious model, and its confident wrong answer
text:
The obvious model, and its confident wrong answer

flat = smf.ols("rise_mm ~ hydration_pct + oven_c", data=d).fit()
print(flat.params.round(4))
print(f"\nR2 = {flat.rsquared:.4f}")

Intercept       -85.0400
hydration_pct     0.6012
oven_c            0.2948
dtype: float64

R2 = 0.3575




best recipe according to this model:  hydration 95.0%,  oven 260 C
...which is the top-right corner of the design.



Both coefficients are positive, so the model’s advice is “as wet and as hot as possible”. A linear model cannot report an interior optimum — it always points at an edge. If your answer is at the boundary of your data, suspect the model before you believe the recommendation.

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
Adding a squared term
\[ y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \varepsilon \]
Differentiate and set to zero: the turning point is at
\[ x^\star = -\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2} \]
and it is a maximum when \(\beta_2 < 0\).

quad = smf.ols("rise_mm ~ hydration_pct + I(hydration_pct**2)", data=d).fit()
b1 = quad.params["hydration_pct"]
b2 = quad.params["I(hydration_pct ** 2)"]

print(f"b1 = {b1:+.4f},  b2 = {b2:+.5f}   (b2 < 0, so it is a hill)")
print(f"peak at -b1/2b2 = {-b1 / (2*b2):.2f} % hydration")
print(f"R2 {flat.rsquared:.4f} -> {quad.rsquared:.4f}")

b1 = +9.2165,  b2 = -0.05681   (b2 < 0, so it is a hill)
peak at -b1/2b2 = 81.11 % hydration
R2 0.3575 -> 0.4122

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
What a quadratic coefficient means

Once \(x^2\) is in the model, \(\beta_1\) is no longer “the effect of \(x\)”. The slope now varies with \(x\):
\[ \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \beta_1 + 2\beta_2 x \]


for h in (65, 75, 85, 92):
    print(f"at {h}% hydration, one more point of water is worth "
          f"{b1 + 2*b2*h:+.3f} mm")

at 65% hydration, one more point of water is worth +1.831 mm
at 75% hydration, one more point of water is worth +0.695 mm
at 85% hydration, one more point of water is worth -0.442 mm
at 92% hydration, one more point of water is worth -1.237 mm



Positive on the way up, negative past the peak. Reporting \(\beta_1\) alone would be reporting the slope at a hydration of zero — a dough made entirely of flour.

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
The question an interaction answers
Is the best oven temperature the same for wet dough as for dry dough?
\[ y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 z + \beta_3 xz + \varepsilon
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{\partial y}{\partial z} = \beta_2 + \beta_3 x \]

\(\beta_3\) is the amount by which the effect of temperature changes per unit of hydration. If it is zero, the two variables act independently and you can give one recommendation for each. If it is not, you cannot.


In a formula: x:z is the interaction alone, x*z expands to x + z + x:z. Prefer x*z — an interaction without its main effects is almost never what you meant.

The ridge runs diagonally. That diagonal is the interaction: wetter dough wants a hotter oven.

text:
What C(baker) does
It adds one dummy per baker (minus a reference), giving each their own intercept. The other coefficients are then estimated within bakers: from variation in hydration among that baker’s own loaves, where skill is held constant because it is the same person.

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
Read those three numbers again


the model without baker effects is off by -4.20 percentage points
and it reports R2 = 0.904



Ninety per cent of the variance explained, every coefficient significant, and a recommendation four points of hydration wrong. Nothing in that model’s own output reveals the problem. The only way to find it was to know the bakers were confounded with the treatment and to control for them.


This is omitted variable bias with a name you can act on. The omitted variable was not unobservable — it was sitting in a column called baker.

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
What fixed effects cost you


Seven parameters for eight bakers. On 240 rows that is affordable; on 24 it would not be.
Between-baker information is discarded. You can no longer ask whether wetter bakers do better, because that comparison is exactly what you removed.
Anything constant within a baker is unidentified. If a baker always used the same flour, its effect and theirs are indistinguishable.



Fixed effects are not free and are not always right. They are the correct tool when you want the within-group effect and suspect the between-group comparison is contaminated.

An optimum estimated from data has uncertainty, and quoting it to two decimal places implies a precision you do not have.

    {"hydration_pct": np.linspace(70, 95, 60), "oven_c": T_TRUE, "baker": "D"}
)).summary_frame()

hs2 = np.linspace(70, 95, 60)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 2.9))
ax.plot(hs2, pred["mean"], color=CL.accent)
ax.fill_between(hs2, pred["mean_ci_lower"], pred["mean_ci_upper"],
                color=CL.accent, alpha=0.18)
ax.axvline(H_TRUE, color=CL.warn, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Hydration (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("Predicted rise (mm)")
plt.show()



The peak is flat. Anything from roughly 82% to 91% is indistinguishable, and that — not a single number — is the honest recommendation.

section: Comparing models, and what AIC is not
text:
Comparing models, and what AIC is not
\[ \mathrm{AIC} = -2\log L + 2k \]
Fit, penalised for parameters. Lower is better, and only relative — an AIC of 1,204 means nothing on its own.

nested_test = smf.ols(FULL.replace(" + hydration_pct:oven_c", ""), data=d).fit()
f_stat, p_val, _ = full.compare_f_test(nested_test)
print(f"F-test for adding the interaction: F = {f_stat:.2f}, p = {p_val:.2e}")
print(f"AIC {nested_test.aic:.1f} -> {full.aic:.1f}")

F-test for adding the interaction: F = 289.08, p = 2.31e-42
AIC 1380.6 -> 1185.5



Two rules. Compare AIC only on identical rows — drop a missing value in one model and the comparison is void. And use the F-test only for nested models; AIC is what you have when they are not.


A model chosen by AIC was chosen by you, using AIC. Reporting it as though the data selected it — and then reporting its \(p\)-values as though you had not looked — is the most common quiet misuse of model comparison.

title: Session 2: Advanced Regression
text:
Key takeaways


A linear model cannot report an interior optimum. If the answer is at the edge of your data, suspect the model.
With \(x^2\) present, \(\beta_1\) is the slope at \(x = 0\). With an interaction present, \(\beta_1\) is the effect when the other variable is zero. Both are usually meaningless values.
An interaction means you cannot give one recommendation. The advice depends on the other variable.
Fixed effects buy you the within-group effect, and they cost parameters, between-group information, and anything constant within a group.
A model can explain 90% of the variance and give advice four points wrong, with nothing in its own output to warn you.

2 · Why a line will not do
Suppose \(y\) is 0 or 1 and you fit \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) anyway.


The fitted values run off to \(\pm\infty\), so you get predicted probabilities above 1 and below 0, which are not probabilities.
The residuals cannot be normal, because for any \(x\) there are only two possible values of \(y\).
The variance of a Bernoulli variable is \(p(1-p)\), which depends on \(p\) — so the variance changes with the fitted value, by construction.



The fix is not a different error assumption. It is to model something that is allowed to be any real number, and then map it into \([0, 1]\).

If an event has probability \(p\), its odds are
\[ \text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p} \]

Log-odds run over the whole line
\[ \text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p} \]

Log-odds are symmetric about zero, unbounded in both directions, and therefore something a linear model can happily produce. So we model those:
\[ \log\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k \]

title: Session 3: Before the session
text:
And back again
Inverting gives the logistic function, which is where the method’s name comes from:
\[ p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}} \]

So a coefficient is a change in log-odds per unit of \(x\). Exponentiate it and you get an odds ratio: the multiplicative factor by which the odds change.
A coefficient of 0.69 means \(e^{0.69} = 2\): the odds double.


A coefficient of 2.0 does not mean the probability doubles. It means the odds are multiplied by \(e^2 \approx 7.4\). What that does to the probability depends entirely on where you started — near \(p = 0.5\) it moves a lot, near \(p = 0.99\) almost nothing.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
What “no unique solution” means
\[ \hat\beta_{\text{OLS}} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y \]
With \(p > n\), \(X^\top X\) is \(200 \times 200\) with rank at most 60. It is singular and cannot be inverted.

There are infinitely many coefficient vectors that fit the training data perfectly. The data cannot choose between them, so we have to add a rule that does. That rule is the penalty, and choosing it is what this session is about.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
The trade
\[ \mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat f(x))^2\right] = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2 \]
Least squares is unbiased, which sounds like a virtue. It buys that unbiasedness with variance, and when \(p\) approaches \(n\) the price becomes absurd.

Every estimator in this session is deliberately biased. Each adds a penalty that pulls coefficients towards zero — knowing that is the wrong place for them — because the variance it saves is worth more than the bias it costs.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
Standardise first, always
A penalty adds up the coefficients. A coefficient’s size depends on its variable’s units, so an unstandardised penalty punishes whichever variable happens to be measured in small units.

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X.values)     # mean 0, sd 1, every column
print(f"column means {np.abs(Xs.mean(0)).max():.2e}, sds {Xs.std(0).min():.4f}")

column means 1.48e-15, sds 1.0000



This is not a nicety. Forget it and your penalty is applied in arbitrary units, and the variables it selects are partly an artefact of how somebody chose to record them.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
The estimator
\[ \hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \; \|y - X\beta\|^2 + \lambda \|\beta\|_2^2 \]
which, unlike OLS, has a closed form that always exists:
\[ \hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y \]

Adding \(\lambda\) to the diagonal makes a singular matrix invertible. Ridge did not merely improve the \(p > n\) problem — it made it solvable.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
Why it never reaches zero
In the singular-value basis, ridge multiplies the \(j\)-th component of the OLS solution by
\[ \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda} \]


That factor is strictly between 0 and 1 for any finite \(\lambda\).
Directions with little variance (\(d_j\) small) are shrunk hardest — which is exactly where OLS was most unstable.
It is never equal to zero, so ridge keeps all 200 coefficients, always.

Two hundred non-zero coefficients, 135 of them large enough to notice. Ridge has not told you which ingredients matter, because it structurally cannot. It gives you a prediction and no list.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
The estimator
\[ \hat\beta_{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \; \|y - X\beta\|^2 + \lambda \|\beta\|_1 \]
One character has changed — \(\ell_2\) to \(\ell_1\) — and the behaviour is qualitatively different.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
Corners produce zeros
Both methods minimise the same squared error subject to a budget on \(\beta\). The shape of the budget is what differs.


The \(\ell_2\) budget \(\{\|\beta\|_2 \le t\}\) is a circle. A circle is smooth, so the point where the error contours first touch it is generically off both axes: no zeros.
The \(\ell_1\) budget \(\{\|\beta\|_1 \le t\}\) is a diamond, with corners on the axes. Contours touching a corner give a solution with a coefficient exactly zero.



Sparsity is a fact about the geometry of the constraint region, not a numerical threshold applied afterwards.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
Soft-thresholding, in one variable
With one standardised predictor, the lasso solution is
\[ \hat\beta = \operatorname{sign}(z)\left(|z| - \lambda\right)_+ \]
where \(z\) is the OLS estimate. Everything within \(\lambda\) of zero becomes zero; everything else moves towards zero by exactly \(\lambda\).


Ridge is a rotation towards zero — always proportional, never arriving. The lasso has a flat stretch, and that flat stretch is variable selection.

What was planted

      f"{X.baking_soda.corr(X.baking_powder):.4f}")

The lasso zeroed one of two ingredients with identical true effects, and gave the survivor most of their combined weight. It does this in every cross-validation split, confidently, and nothing in the output hints that a second ingredient is hiding behind the first.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
Why it has no choice

The \(\ell_1\) penalty charges for \(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|\). Two near-identical columns can deliver the same fit by loading everything onto one of them — which costs the same total but is a corner of the diamond, and corners are where the solution lands. Splitting evenly costs the same and is not a corner.


Ridge does the opposite: the \(\ell_2\) penalty charges for \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2\), and that is minimised by splitting the load. Ridge would share it and select neither.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
The estimator
\[ \hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \|y - X\beta\|^2 + \lambda\left(\alpha\|\beta\|_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2\right) \]


\(\alpha = 1\) is the lasso. \(\alpha = 0\) is ridge.
The \(\ell_1\) part still produces exact zeros.
The \(\ell_2\) part has no reason to prefer either of two identical columns, so it shares between them.



In scikit-learn \(\alpha\) is called l1_ratio. In glmnet it is called alpha, and scikit-learn’s alpha is the overall \(\lambda\). This has caused a great deal of confusion; check which library you are reading.

The grouping effect, measured

CV seed 4:  soda +0.552   powder +1.358   sum +1.910



The sum is stable. The split is not — it moves with an arbitrary choice of cross-validation seed. Two collinear columns carry one identifiable quantity between them, and no penalty conjures a second. The elastic net’s real service is telling you there are two ingredients; it cannot tell you how to divide the credit.

This is not a failure. Cross-validation tunes for prediction, and the penalty that predicts best is smaller than the penalty that selects best. Keeping a few extra small coefficients costs almost nothing in error and can help.


A lasso’s non-zero set is not a list of true effects. Reporting it as one — “the model identified 20 drivers of taste” — is the commonest misuse of this method, and it is a misuse of a correct model.

The weakest planted effect is not recovered by anything, and at 60 observations it should not be — it sits below the detection floor. No choice of method rescues a signal the sample size cannot support, and a method that appears to has found noise.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
section: Three limitations to state out loud
text:
Three limitations to state out loud


Penalised coefficients are biased, by design. Do not report them as effect sizes without saying so.
The standard errors in the output are not valid after a data-driven selection. There is no honest \(p\)-value on a lasso coefficient without extra machinery — post-selection inference, or a sample split.
Selection is unstable under collinearity. Which of two correlated variables survives is close to arbitrary, and it changes with a resample.



Limitation 2 is not academic. A published table of lasso-selected coefficients with stars beside them is reporting inference that was invalidated by the selection that produced the table.

title: Session 4: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net
text:
Key takeaways


When \(p > n\), OLS fits perfectly and predicts terribly. Training error of zero is a symptom, not an achievement.
Every method here is biased on purpose, and that is why it wins.
Standardise before penalising, or the penalty is in arbitrary units.
Ridge shrinks and never zeroes. The lasso zeroes, because the \(\ell_1\) ball has corners.
The lasso must choose between collinear columns; the elastic net shares. But the split is not identified — only the pair’s total.
Cross-validation optimises prediction. Its selected set is not a list of true effects, and its coefficients have no valid \(p\)-values.

title: Session 5: Before the session

2 · The best possible classifier
Suppose you knew, for every point \(x\), the true probability of each class. The best rule is obvious: predict the most likely class.
\[ \hat y(x) = \arg\max_j \Pr(Y = j \mid X = x) \]
That is the Bayes classifier, and no method can beat it. Its error rate is the Bayes rate, and it is usually not zero — because classes overlap, and because labels contain mistakes.

This session’s data is generated from known distributions, so the Bayes rate can be computed exactly. You will know, before fitting anything, the accuracy no classifier can exceed.


Which means: if your test accuracy comes out above that number, you have a leak — test data in your training set, or a feature that encodes the answer. Knowing the floor turns “my model scores 0.99” from good news into a bug report.

text:
3 · \(k\)-nearest neighbours, by hand
The whole algorithm: to classify a new point, find the \(k\) closest training points and take a vote.
There is no fitting. There are no coefficients. The training data is the model.
\[ \hat{\Pr}(Y = j \mid x) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in N_k(x)} \mathbb{1}(y_i = j) \]

\(k = n\): every prediction is the majority class. The boundary has vanished. High bias.
Somewhere in between is a \(k\) that is close to the truth.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
Why they come out negative
Suppose cohort 4’s effect is still growing in quarter 8, and we use cohort 4 as the control group for cohort 7.


Cohort 7’s outcome rises, because its cat just arrived.
Cohort 4’s outcome also rises — because its effect is still growing.
Difference-in-differences subtracts the control’s change from the treated group’s change.
So it subtracts cohort 4’s ongoing treatment effect, and books it as evidence that treatment does nothing — or, if the control’s growth is faster, as evidence of harm.



The control group’s own treatment effect is being subtracted from the treated group’s. That is the whole bug, and one treatment dummy cannot see it.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
Two conditions, both needed


Staggered adoption. With one common treatment date there are no already-treated controls and TWFE is fine.
Effects that change over time or differ across cohorts. With one constant effect everywhere, subtracting the control’s effect subtracts the same number from both sides and it cancels.



Both hold in this data — and both hold in most real policy rollouts, which is why this matters. Dynamic effects are the normal case. Almost nothing works fully on its first day.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
Group-time average treatment effects
Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) refuse to pool. Instead of one \(\beta\), estimate one effect for each cohort \(g\) in each period \(t\):
\[ \text{ATT}(g, t) = \mathbb{E}\left[Y_t(g) - Y_t(0) \mid G = g\right] \]
Each is a clean 2×2, using as controls only units that are not yet treated at time \(t\) — never the already-treated.

cs = dd.CallawaySantAnna(control_group="not_yet_treated").fit(
    d, outcome="dwell_min", unit="cafe_id", time="quarter",
    first_treat="cat_arrival_quarter", aggregate="group")

print(f"overall ATT   {cs.overall_att:+.4f}")
print(f"TWFE          {twfe.params['has_cat']:+.4f}")

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
section: This is the most important slide in the session
text:
This is the most important slide in the session


Callaway–Sant’Anna returns NA for those cells, because the data cannot answer.
Two-way fixed effects reported a number for them — with three stars — by quietly using already-treated cafés as controls.



An estimator that refuses is more useful than one that invents. The nine NAs are not a shortcoming of the method; they are a correct description of what this research design can and cannot support.


And it is a lesson about design, not software. If you plan a rollout where everything is treated by the end of your data, you have planned a study that cannot evaluate its own last phase. Keeping a control group untreated is a decision made before any data exists.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
section: Stop testing the assumption. Bound it.
text:
Stop testing the assumption. Bound it.
Parallel trends is untestable, so Rambachan and Roth (2023) propose a better question:

How large would a violation have to be before my conclusion changes?

Suppose the treated cohort was on a differential trend of \(\delta\) minutes per quarter. It contaminates \(\text{ATT}(g,t)\) by roughly \(\delta \times (t - g + 1)\). Solve for the \(\delta\) that drives the estimate to zero — the breakdown value.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
Computing it

for g, v in cs.group_effects.items():
    n_q = len(cells[(cells.cohort == g) & (cells.event_time >= 0)
                    & cells.est.notna()])
    mean_exposure = np.arange(1, n_q + 1).mean()
    print(f"cohort {g:2d}:  ATT {v['effect']:+7.3f}   "
          f"mean exposure {mean_exposure:.1f} quarters   "
          f"breakdown δ = {v['effect'] / mean_exposure:+.3f} min/quarter")

slope = np.polyfit(pre.event_time, pre.est, 1)[0]
print(f"\nobserved pre-treatment trend slope: {slope:+.4f} min/quarter")

cohort  7:  ATT  +3.009   mean exposure 2.0 quarters   breakdown δ = +1.504 min/quarter

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
section: Which gives you a sentence you can defend
text:
Which gives you a sentence you can defend

“To explain away the cohort-4 effect, the treated cafés would have to have been on a differential trend of 3.85 minutes per quarter. The trend we can measure before adoption is 0.04 minutes per quarter — nearly ninety times smaller. A violation of the required size would have been unmissable in the pre-period.”


That is a far stronger claim than “pre-trends look parallel”, and it is the form the current literature expects. diff_diff implements the full Rambachan–Roth procedure as dd.HonestDiD; the arithmetic above is the same idea, done by hand so you can see what it rests on.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
The rest of the toolkit
The same problem produced several estimators. They mostly agree, and knowing they exist matters more than knowing which to prefer:







Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021)
group-time ATTs, not-yet-treated controls


Sun & Abraham (2021)
interaction-weighted event study


Borusyak, Jaravel & Spiess (2024)
impute \(Y(0)\) from untreated observations


de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020)
robust to treatment switching off


Gardner (2022)
two-stage: remove the fixed effects, then estimate


Arkhangelsky et al. (2021)
synthetic DiD — weights units and periods




All of these are in diff_diff. Try two, and report both.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
What to report


The design first: who is treated, when, and what serves as the control
A decomposition if you use TWFE at all, showing the forbidden weight
Group-time effects, or a stated reason for pooling
An event study, with the pre-period read as a set of tests rather than one
What is not identified, explicitly
A breakdown value, not an assertion that trends look parallel



A DiD result with no event study, no decomposition and no named control group is an interaction coefficient wearing the word “causal”.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
Key takeaways


The interaction in a 2×2 is the DiD estimate. Everything else is that idea under complications.
Under staggered adoption, TWFE is a weighted average of 2×2s — and some weights are negative.
The bug is already-treated units used as controls. When effects grow, the control’s own effect gets subtracted from the treated group’s.
It needs staggered adoption and dynamic or heterogeneous effects. Both are the normal case.
Group-time estimators recover the truth by never making forbidden comparisons.
Read pre-trends as multiple tests, not one star at a time.
An estimator that returns NA is doing you a favour.
Report a breakdown value. “Trends look parallel” is not a robustness check.

title: Session 6: Causal Inference
text:
Where this leaves you

You now have a toolkit that runs from a single straight line to an estimator that knows the limits of its own identification. The through-line has been the same in all six sessions: the fit statistic is not the diagnostic, and the confident answer is the one to check.


Session 1’s regression fitted at \(R^2 = 0.96\) and reported a meaningless slope. This session’s estimator reported the wrong sign at \(p = 10^{-5}\). In both cases the output looked excellent. In both cases the way to find out was to ask what the method was actually comparing.
